title: Dignities describe a named historical convention
text: Lilly distinguishes domicile, exaltation, triplicity, term and face. His examples include Saturn in Capricorn and Jupiter in Sagittarius. Triplicity depends on day or night: the Sun in Aries receives exaltation by day and night, but its fire-triplicity dignity belongs to daytime. A planet’s dignity is a testimony within a question or nativity, not an outcome probability for an arbitrary moment.

title: Same-sign combustion and the cazimi exception
text: The inspected Lilly transcription states an 8°30′ combustion distance with a same-sign condition, 17° for being under the beams, and a 17′ cazimi exception. Its Jupiter-at-28° / Sun-at-18° example is 10° apart and conflicts with the printed 8°30′ rule. The new reading names that textual rule and displays the legacy angular-only convention separately; neither the transcription inconsistency nor the implementation difference is concealed.

title: Apparent retrograde motion
text: Lilly describes direct motion as advancing in zodiacal degrees and retrograde motion as decreasing in degree. The application computes apparent geocentric angular speed. A negative speed does not mean that the planet reverses its heliocentric orbit. The direct/retrograde dignity category is historical interpretation; the measured motion is astronomy.

title: Agrippa’s multi-condition celestial checklist
text: Agrippa II.29 asks the reader to consider planetary positions, motions, aspects, signs and degrees in relation to the observer; he also discusses dignities, day and hour rulers, the Moon and Mercury. A displayed hour-ruler match satisfies only that named comparison. It does not establish that the complete celestial election is suitable, and the chapter gives no universal numerical score.

title: Two reported planetary-hour conventions
text: Agrippa II.34 reports dividing sunrise to sunset into twelve equal daylight intervals, and sunset to the next sunrise into twelve night intervals. It also describes a competing method based on successive 15° ecliptic ascensions and local oblique-ascension tables. The Workbench implements the former. Planetary hours can differ in length from civil clock hours and may be unavailable where the needed sunrise or sunset does not occur.

title: Tithi is a Moon–Sun angle, not a midnight date
text: Rao’s §1.3.8.1 divides the normalized Moon-minus-Sun longitude difference into thirty 12° intervals. Example 2 uses Moon 84°12′ and Sun 227°46′: the normalized difference is 216°26′, giving tithi 19, Krishna Chaturthi. This is a worked arithmetic example, not a dated event or evidence of an outcome. A tithi can change within one civil date.

title: Nakṣatra and ayanāṃśa
text: The selected textbook divides the sidereal zodiac into twenty-seven equal nakṣatra sectors of 13°20′, with four 3°20′ pādas each. Its ayanāṃśa section acknowledges competing conventions and selects Chitrapaksha/Lahiri. The Workbench uses an explicitly approximate linear Lahiri model. Tropical and sidereal sign labels can differ for the same planet without disagreement about the underlying sky.

title: A named equal-hora convention
text: Rao §1.3.11 divides the sunrise-to-next-sunrise interval into twenty-four equal horas, beginning with the sunrise weekday ruler and continuing in Chaldean order. This differs from twelve daylight and twelve night intervals when day and night lengths differ. Neither method should silently replace the other. The local comparison divides actual computed sunrise intervals rather than assuming exactly sixty civil minutes.

title: A corrected attribution for the greater Dog star
text: The inspected 1651 English text of Agrippa II.31 calls the greater Dog star Venereal, meaning Venus in its symbolic scheme. This supports the inherited Venus attribution and contradicts an old repository skill example attributing Jupiter/Mars to Agrippa. The text’s historical seventh degree of Cancer must not be reused as a present-day longitude. The modern name identification has its own ESA/Hubble source chunk.

title: The Dog Star is Sirius
text: ESA/Hubble image record heic0516a identifies Sirius A as the Dog Star and places the Sirius system in Canis Major. This astronomical naming evidence is separate from a historical author’s symbolic planetary-nature attribution; it does not validate a Venus-like physical influence or a current stellar longitude.

title: Agreement can share one calculation
text: Moon phase, tithi and several lunar rules reuse the same Sun and Moon longitudes. Their agreement is a mathematical dependency, not independent corroboration or evidence of predictive validity. Calendar date labels, tropical signs and sidereal sectors also have different reference frames and day boundaries; compare their conventions before calling a difference a calculation error.

title: Layered instrument design
text: The Met identifies its object 444408 as a brass and silver astrolabe made in Yemen in 1291 CE. Engraved circular scales and layered star pointers offer a design reference for a modern interactive instrument. The object is not evidence for a modern heliocentric simulation, and the new screen should label its own projection and scale.
